questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: Sita buys a packet from a shop. The packet carries an expiry date and a printed price. Explain what she can do if the contents turn out to be defective, and what she can do if the shopkeeper asks more than the printed price.

markingPoints.description: A product defective well within the expiry period can be replaced on request
Selling above the printed price on the packet can be protested and complained about
A consumer can bargain with the seller to sell at less than the MRP

answerScheme.modelAnswer: If the product is defective and still well within the expiry period, Sita can ask for a replacement. If the shopkeeper sells the good above the printed price on the packet — the MRP, or maximum retail price — she can protest and complain. A consumer can also bargain with the seller to sell at less than the MRP.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A shop in your locality sells packaged goods and medicines. Show, step by step, what happens when a customer finds a product defective well within its expiry period, when the expiry period is not printed on the pack at all, when the shop is selling medicines that have already expired, and when a good is sold for more than the price printed on the packet.

markingPoints.description: A product defective well within the expiry period can be taken back and a replacement asked for
If the expiry period was not printed the manufacturer blames the shopkeeper and will not accept the responsibility
Severe action can be taken against anyone selling medicines that have expired
A consumer can protest and complain if a good is sold above the price printed on the packet
The printed price is the MRP and a consumer can bargain with the seller to sell at less than it

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1: A product defective well within the expiry period can be taken back and a replacement asked for. Step 2: If the expiry period was not printed, the manufacturer blames the shopkeeper and will not accept the responsibility. Step 3: Severe action can be taken against anyone selling medicines that have expired. Step 4: A consumer can protest and complain if a good is sold above the price printed on the packet. Step 5: That price is the MRP, and a consumer can bargain to be sold at less than it.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
Ramesh buys a packet of biscuits from a shop near his colony. The packet carries a printed price and an expiry date, and the biscuits turn out to be broken. He also notices that the shopkeeper is asking customers more than the price printed on the packet. Across the road, another shop sells medicines, and Ramesh sees sealed packets whose expiry dates have already passed. The shopkeeper tells him there is nothing wrong with them, since they are still sealed.

(a) Ramesh's biscuits are broken, but the expiry date on the packet has not passed. What can he ask the shop for? (b) The shopkeeper is asking more than the price printed on the packet. What can Ramesh do about that, and what is the printed price called? (c) Ramesh sees sealed medicine packets in the other shop whose expiry dates have already passed. Analyse how far a consumer's protection depends on what is actually printed on the packet.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) He can ask for a replacement, since the goods are defective well within the expiry period. (b) He can protest and complain, as the packet carries the MRP, the maximum retail price. (c) Where the expiry period is not printed the manufacturer blames the shopkeeper and refuses responsibility, while selling expired medicines invites severe action.

questions.stem:
Abirami is a student of Ansari Nagar. She joins a two-year course at a local coaching institute for professional courses in New Delhi, and at the time of joining pays the fees Rs 61,020 as a lump sum for the entire course of two years. After one year she decides to opt out, as she finds the quality of teaching is not up to the mark, and asks for a refund of the fee for one year. The institute denies it. She takes the matter to the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.

(a) How did Abirami pay for the course, and why did she decide to opt out after one year? (b) What did the Commission direct the institute to do, how much was it, and what reason did the commission give? (c) Analyse what that decision shows about a student's freedom to choose when an institute has already taken the whole fee for the course in advance.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) She paid Rs 61,020 as a lump sum for the entire two-year course, and left because the quality of teaching was not up to the mark. (b) It directed a refund of Rs 28,000, saying that she had the right to choose. (c) The institute cannot keep the whole fee once a student stops attending, so a student keeps the right to leave.
